title: SEBI Just Rewrote India's Mutual Fund Rulebook. Your Fund Manager Now Has to Invest 20 Per Cent of Their Salary in Their Own Schemes.
excerpt: The new regulations, effective since April 1, cap expense ratios, slash brokerage fees by up to 85 per cent, enforce portfolio overlap limits, and require fund managers to put their own money where their advice is. For NRI investors holding Indian mutual funds, every line item just changed.
body:
India's Securities and Exchange Board — SEBI — has replaced its 30-year-old mutual fund regulations with a comprehensive new framework that touches every aspect of how funds charge fees, deploy capital, and disclose performance. The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026, effective since April 1, represent the most significant overhaul of India's ₹82-lakh-crore mutual fund industry since the original rules were written in 1996.

For the estimated 1.5 million NRIs who hold Indian mutual fund investments — through direct plans, NRE/NRO accounts, or the new GIFT City funds — these changes are not abstract. They directly affect what you pay, what your fund manager is incentivised to do, and how transparent your holdings are.

## Lower Fees, by Law

The headline change is a restructured expense ratio framework. SEBI has introduced a Base Expense Ratio (BER) that separates core management fees from taxes, statutory levies, and transaction costs. This is designed to end the practice of funds burying non-investment expenses inside the total expense ratio, which made it difficult for investors to compare true management costs across funds.

The maximum total expense ratio has been capped at 2.25 per cent for equity schemes on the first ₹500 crore of assets, declining on a sliding scale as assets under management grow. For large funds — the ones most NRI investors hold — this means a meaningful reduction in annual costs. SEBI has also slashed brokerage caps from 12 basis points to as low as 2 basis points for cash market trades, and capped derivatives brokerage at 6 to 12 basis points depending on the instrument.

The cumulative effect is significant. On a ₹50 lakh NRI portfolio in Indian equity funds, the fee reduction could save ₹15,000 to ₹40,000 per year, depending on fund size and category. Over a 10-year horizon, the compounding impact of lower fees on returns is substantial.

## Skin in the Game

Perhaps the most consequential change is the new requirement for fund managers to invest at least 20 per cent of their salary in the schemes they manage. This is SEBI's version of the "skin in the game" principle — the idea that a fund manager who has their own money at risk will make different decisions than one who is simply collecting a management fee.

The regulation applies to key investment personnel, not just the named fund manager. It covers the Chief Investment Officer, fund managers, and other designated employees involved in investment decisions. The investment must be made in the specific schemes they manage, not in any fund from the same AMC.

For NRI investors, this is a structural improvement. One of the persistent criticisms of Indian mutual funds has been the misalignment between fund manager incentives and investor outcomes. A manager earning ₹2 crore per year who must invest ₹40 lakh of their own salary in their own fund is likely to think twice about excessive risk-taking or closet indexing.

## Portfolio Overlap Limits

SEBI has introduced a 50 per cent overlap cap between schemes from the same AMC. This targets a common industry practice: launching multiple funds with different names but substantially identical portfolios. An investor who thought they were diversifying by holding a large-cap fund and a flexi-cap fund from the same AMC may have been holding 60 to 70 per cent of the same stocks.

Under the new rules, if two schemes from the same fund house share more than 50 per cent of their portfolio, the AMC must either merge them or restructure. For NRI investors who often hold multiple schemes from the same provider for convenience, this is a welcome change — it forces genuine diversification.

## Tighter IPO Oversight

Separately, SEBI is also tightening oversight of how companies use equity capital raised from public markets. Draft proposals reviewed by Reuters would lower the mandatory monitoring threshold from ₹100 crore to ₹50 crore, require credit rating agencies to report directly to stock exchanges on fund usage, and introduce penalties of ₹50,000 per violation for companies that obstruct monitoring.

The timing is deliberate. India's IPO pipeline stands at a record ₹2.5 trillion across 190 approved companies, but only 15 have come to market since January due to the Middle East conflict-driven selloff. When the pipeline reopens, SEBI wants tighter governance in place. For NRI investors who participate in Indian IPOs — either directly or through mutual fund allocations — this means greater accountability on where their capital goes after listing.

## What NRI Investors Should Do

The new regulations do not require NRI investors to take immediate action, but they do warrant a portfolio review. Check the expense ratios on your existing holdings — some funds will have already adjusted fees downward since April 1. Look for overlap across your Indian fund holdings; if you hold three or four schemes from the same AMC, the new rules may trigger mergers or restructuring that affect your positions.

For new investments, the GIFT City fund ecosystem — which allows NRIs to invest in Indian markets through USD-denominated vehicles without the regulatory friction of NRE/NRO accounts — now operates under the same updated framework. Four GIFT City funds are currently active, and the lower fee structure applies equally.

SEBI's message is clear: as India's mutual fund industry grows beyond ₹82 lakh crore, the regulatory framework is evolving to match. For NRI investors, the changes are overwhelmingly positive — lower costs, better alignment, and more transparency. The 30-year-old rulebook is gone. The replacement is built for an industry that is now the backbone of India's domestic capital markets.
author: Diaspora Desk
